newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Palestinians frantically get rid of shekels.
newsitem.headline: Palestinians frantically get rid of shekels.

text.p: Palestinians are rushing to dump their shekels as the Israeli currency plunged to a new low at the end of last week, businessmen and economists said on Sunday.
But Palestinian foreign currency changers say they have refrained from selling large amounts of Jordanian dinars and dollars because they do not expect the shekel to continue depreciating.

"People became frantic on Saturday after the shekel tumbled against the Jordanian dinar and the dollar as a result of the Israeli government's exchange rate reforms," said Ibrahim al-Fuqaha, financial consultant at the Azzon exchange office in Nablus.
"These Israeli financial measures have hurt Palestinians, especially those who work in Israel and get paid in shekels," al-Fuqaha told Reuters.

The Palestinian economy is closely linked to Israel's, with tens of thousands of Palestinians working in Israel everyday and most trade conducted with the Jewish state. With no currency of their own, Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza Strip do business in the shekel, the Jordanian dinar and the dollar.

But the Israeli cabinet's decision in mid-June to adjust the shekel's exchange rate band and crawling slope set off a wave of speculation in Israel that has brought the shekel to a low of 3.592 to the dollar on Friday, a drop of about five percent.
Against the dinar, the shekel traded at 6.00 on Sunday.

"Changes in the value of the Israeli shekel lead to inflation, and it affects our companies' assets," said Safwan al-Batayneh, director of the embroyonic Palestinian Securities Exchange. "But I don't expect it to have a great impact on activity in the stock market, which is limited anyway."
"Inflation usually pushes traders to invest in shares and property because it is safer," Batayneh said.
"We have to separate our economy from the Israeli economy, so we won't have to pay the price for crisis and fluctuations in the Israeli economy," he said.
Vegetable vendor Kamal Abu Tharifeh said produce prices had not increased after the shekel began to weaken but people have been buying less.
"My sales have fallen by 30 to 50 percent in the last week," he said.
